title: Environment & Configuration
subtitle: process.env, dotenv, config modules, and NODE_ENV branching
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Applications need different settings for different environments (dev, test, production) — database URLs, API keys, port numbers. Hardcoding these in source code is insecure (secrets in git) and inflexible.
whyItExists.solution: Store configuration in environment variables (process.env). In development, use a .env file with the dotenv package to set those variables locally without committing them. Production environment sets them via the hosting platform.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every Node.js application. Always externalize secrets (API keys, DB passwords, JWT secrets) and environment-specific values (port, db URL, log level) via env vars.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use env vars for non-secret, non-varying configuration (app name, supported locales). Those belong in config files committed to the repo.

explainModes.beginner: process.env is an object containing all environment variables — settings passed to Node from the operating system or a .env file. You read them with process.env.MY_KEY. If the variable isn't set, you get undefined — use a default: process.env.PORT || '3000'. The dotenv package loads a .env file into process.env automatically.
explainModes.simple: process.env.NODE_ENV: 'development', 'test', 'production' (set by the framework or CI). process.env.PORT: which port to listen on. .env file: KEY=VALUE pairs, one per line. dotenv: require('dotenv').config() loads .env. Never commit .env! Add to .gitignore. Default values: const port = process.env.PORT || 3000. Validation: if (!process.env.DB_URL) throw new Error('DB_URL env var required').
explainModes.standard: Config module pattern: create a config.js that reads process.env once, validates required vars, and exports a typed config object. All other files import config — no process.env scattered everywhere. NODE_ENV branching: if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') { /* strict settings */ }. dotenv/config shorthand: node -r dotenv/config server.js (no code change needed). In production: set env vars via hosting platform (Railway, Render, Heroku Config Vars, AWS Secrets Manager). Never log secrets.
explainModes.technical: dotenv internals: reads .env, parses KEY=VALUE (handles quotes, multiline, comments), calls process.env[key] = value. dotenv-expand: supports variable interpolation: BASE_URL=$HOST:$PORT. Secret management in production: env vars in containers (Kubernetes Secrets, Docker secrets), AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler. These mount secrets as env vars at runtime so nothing is in the image. process.env is a plain object — adding/modifying it: process.env.MY_KEY = 'value'. This affects the current process only.
explainModes.deepDive: Security: env vars are visible to child processes and in /proc/self/environ on Linux — not secret from other processes on the same host. For production secrets, prefer a secrets manager that injects at runtime and supports rotation. dotenv-safe: like dotenv but requires all variables listed in .env.example — prevents deploying with missing config. Config schema validation: use Zod or Joi to validate and type-cast env vars at startup. Example: const schema = z.object({ PORT: z.string().transform(Number), DB_URL: z.string().url() }); const config = schema.parse(process.env). This catches misconfiguration at startup, not at the point of use.

content.code:
# .env — development only, NEVER commit this file
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000
DB_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb
JWT_SECRET=super-secret-dev-key-change-in-production
ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173,http://localhost:3000
LOG_LEVEL=debug

content.text: Always add `.env` to your `.gitignore`. Instead, commit a `.env.example` file with all the variable names but no real values — it documents what config is needed without exposing secrets.

questions.question: Why should you never hardcode API keys or database passwords in your Node.js source code?
options: It makes the code run slower because the values are longer
Hardcoded secrets end up in version control — accessible to anyone with repo access, including in git history even after deletion
Node.js cannot read hardcoded strings — it only reads environment variables
It prevents you from using TypeScript
questions.explanation: Once a secret is committed to git, it's in the history permanently — removing it from the latest commit doesn't erase it. If the repo is ever public or leaked, all historical secrets are exposed. Environment variables keep secrets out of the codebase: each environment (dev, staging, prod) provides its own values via the hosting platform or a .env file that's git-ignored.

faq.q: How do I use dotenv in a Node.js project?
faq.a: 1. `npm install dotenv`. 2. Create `.env` with KEY=VALUE entries. 3. Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. 4. At the very top of your entry file (before any other requires): `require('dotenv').config()`. Now process.env has all the values from .env. In production, don't use dotenv — set env vars directly in your hosting platform (Render Config Vars, Railway Variables, AWS Parameter Store, etc.).

examples: Render, Railway, Vercel — all have a Config Vars / Environment Variables UI for production secrets
process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' — disable stack traces in error responses
GitHub Actions: secrets stored as encrypted env vars, injected at CI runtime
